title: German 1
description: Free German 1 study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Greetings & Pronunciation

concepts.intro: German has two ways to say 'you': the formal Sie and the informal du. This choice shapes which greetings you use.
b: Use Sie with strangers, elders, and in business ("Wie geht es Ihnen?")
Use du with friends, family, children, and peers ("Wie geht's?")
Sie is always capitalized, even mid-sentence
Germans switch to du less readily than English speakers switch to first names
When in doubt, start with Sie and let the other person offer du

concepts.intro: German greetings often change with the time of day.
b: Guten Morgen – good morning (until ~10-11am)
Guten Tag – good day/hello (daytime, most common)
Guten Abend – good evening
Gute Nacht – good night (only when parting, not a greeting)
Hallo and Servus (regional) work any time informally

concepts.intro: Farewells also split along the formal/informal line.
b: Auf Wiedersehen – formal goodbye
Tschüss – informal goodbye, very common
Bis bald / Bis später – see you soon / see you later
Ciao is used informally, borrowed from Italian
Mach's gut – informal, casual 'take care'

concepts.intro: Three small words carry a lot of social weight.
b: Danke – thank you; Danke schön – thank you very much
Bitte – please, and also 'you're welcome'
Entschuldigung – excuse me / sorry, used to get attention or apologize
Bitte schön / Gern geschehen – you're welcome (extra polite)
Es tut mir leid – I'm sorry (for something more serious)

concepts.intro: German vowel sounds differ from English and must be learned by sound, not by English spelling instinct.
b: ä sounds like 'e' in 'bed' (Mädchen)
ö has no English equivalent; round lips and say 'e' (schön)
ü has no English equivalent; round lips and say 'ee' (müde)
ie is a long 'ee' sound (wie, Sie); ei is like English 'eye' (nein, Wein)
ß (Eszett) represents a sharp 's' sound, used after long vowels/diphthongs (Straße, groß)

concepts.intro: A handful of consonants are pronounced very differently from English.
b: w is pronounced like English v (Wasser sounds like 'VAH-ser')
v is usually pronounced like English f (Vater sounds like 'FAH-ter')
z is always pronounced 'ts' (Zeit sounds like 'tsyte')
ch after a/o/u is a throaty sound (Bach); after e/i/consonants it's softer (ich)
sch is pronounced like English 'sh' (Schule)

keyFacts: All German nouns are capitalized, no matter where they appear in a sentence.
Sie (capital S) is the formal 'you' for one person or many; du is informal singular.
ß stands for a sharp 's' sound after long vowels or diphthongs; it never appears after short vowels.
Word stress in native German words usually falls on the first syllable (HAL-lo, GU-ten Tag).
traps: Saying 'Wie heißen du?' instead of 'Wie heißt du?' — du takes the -t ending, not -en.
Pronouncing w like English w — it should sound like English v, so Wasser is 'VAH-ser', not 'WAH-ser'.
Using du with strangers, older people, or in formal settings — this can sound rude; use Sie until invited to use du.
Confusing bitte (please/you're welcome) with danke (thank you) — they are opposites in function, not synonyms.

units.name: Articles & Cases Intro

concepts.intro: Every German noun has a grammatical gender — masculine, feminine, or neuter — shown by its article.
b: der = masculine (der Mann, der Tisch)
die = feminine (die Frau, die Tür)
das = neuter (das Kind, das Buch)
Gender is often not logical: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter, not feminine
You must memorize the article together with each new noun

concepts.intro: Definite articles (der/die/das) mean 'the'; indefinite articles (ein/eine/ein) mean 'a/an'.
b: Masculine: der Hund → ein Hund
Feminine: die Katze → eine Katze
Neuter: das Auto → ein Auto
Indefinite articles have no plural form (Autos, not 'eine Autos')
kein negates a noun that would take ein/eine: kein Hund, keine Katze

concepts.intro: The nominative case marks the subject of the sentence — the one doing the action.
b: Der Mann liest. – The man is reading. (der Mann = subject)
Die Frau arbeitet. – The woman works.
Das Kind spielt. – The child plays.
Question word: Wer? (Who?) asks for the nominative subject
Nominative articles: der, die, das, die (plural)

concepts.intro: The accusative case marks the direct object — the thing or person receiving the action.
b: Only the masculine article changes: der → den
Ich sehe den Mann. – I see the man.
Feminine, neuter, and plural stay the same: die Frau/die Frau, das Kind/das Kind
Ich habe einen Hund. – ein → einen in the masculine accusative
Question word: Wen? / Was? (Whom?/What?) asks for the accusative object

concepts.intro: No matter the original gender, all plural nouns use the same definite article.
b: die Männer – the men
die Frauen – the women
die Kinder – the children
die Bücher – the books
Plural endings vary (-e, -er, -n/-en, -s, or none) and must be learned per noun

concepts.intro: Pronouns replace nouns and must match the noun's gender and number.
b: ich (I), du (you, informal), er/sie/es (he/she/it)
wir (we), ihr (you all, informal), sie/Sie (they/you formal)
der Mann → er; die Frau → sie; das Kind → es
Pronoun gender always matches the noun's grammatical gender, even for objects
Der Tisch ist groß. Er ist braun. – The table is big. It is brown.

keyFacts: Only the masculine definite article changes in the accusative: der → den (die, das, and plural die stay the same).
Every noun's gender must be memorized individually — it is not predictable from meaning.
ein/eine/ein has no plural form; kein is its negative and does have a plural (keine).
Pronouns (er/sie/es) match the grammatical gender of the noun they replace, not real-world gender.
traps: Saying 'Ich habe ein Hund' instead of 'Ich habe einen Hund' — masculine accusative needs einen, not ein.
Assuming das Mädchen (girl) is feminine because of its meaning — it is neuter because it ends in -chen.
Using der for every noun by default — die and das nouns are just as common and must be learned separately.
Forgetting that die is used for ALL plural nouns, regardless of the noun's singular gender.

units.name: Regular Verbs

concepts.intro: Regular (weak) verbs are conjugated by removing -en from the infinitive to find the stem, then adding endings.
b: spielen → stem: spiel-
machen → stem: mach-
lernen → stem: lern-
wohnen → stem: wohn-
The stem never changes for regular verbs, unlike irregular verbs

concepts.intro: The same six endings attach to the stem of every regular verb.
b: ich spiel-e
du spiel-st
er/sie/es spiel-t
wir spiel-en
ihr spiel-t
sie/Sie spiel-en

concepts.intro: Verbs like arbeiten (to work) insert an extra -e- before -st and -t endings for easier pronunciation.
b: arbeiten → stem: arbeit-
du arbeit-e-st (not arbeitst)
er/sie/es arbeit-e-t (not arbeitt)
Other examples: reden (to talk) → du redest; finden (to find) → du findest
The wir/sie/Sie forms are unaffected: wir arbeiten

concepts.intro: A core set of everyday regular verbs to memorize.
b: machen – to do/make
kaufen – to buy
kochen – to cook
sagen – to say
fragen – to ask
hören – to hear/listen

concepts.intro: A simple German sentence needs a subject and a conjugated verb, in that order for statements.
b: Ich lerne Deutsch. – I learn German.
Du spielst Fußball. – You play soccer.
Wir wohnen in Berlin. – We live in Berlin.
The conjugated verb must always match its subject
Word order: Subject + Verb + rest of sentence

concepts.intro: nicht (not) negates verbs and most sentence elements.
b: Ich spiele nicht. – I don't play.
Er arbeitet heute nicht. – He isn't working today.
nicht usually comes after the verb and object, but before adjectives/adverbs
Compare with kein, which negates nouns: Ich habe kein Buch.
Ich lerne nicht gern. – I don't like learning.

keyFacts: Find the stem of a regular verb by dropping -en from the infinitive, then add the ending for each person.
The six present-tense endings are: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en for ich/du/er-sie-es/wir/ihr/sie-Sie.
Verbs whose stem ends in -t or -d insert an extra -e- before -st/-t (du arbeitest, not du arbeitst).
The conjugated verb occupies the second position in a simple German statement.
traps: Leaving the verb unconjugated: 'Ich spielen' is wrong — it must be 'Ich spiele'.
Using -st for er/sie/es: 'er spielst' is wrong — it must be 'er spielt'.
Dropping the extra -e- with -t/-d stems: 'du arbeitst' is wrong — it must be 'du arbeitest'.
Confusing nicht (negates verbs/adjectives) with kein (negates nouns with an article): 'Ich habe nicht Buch' is wrong — it must be 'Ich habe kein Buch'.

units.name: Sein & Haben

concepts.intro: sein is one of the most important and most irregular German verbs.
b: ich bin – I am
du bist – you are (informal)
er/sie/es ist – he/she/it is
wir sind – we are
ihr seid – you all are (informal)
sie/Sie sind – they/you (formal) are

concepts.intro: haben is the other essential irregular verb, used for possession and idioms.
b: ich habe – I have
du hast – you have (informal)
er/sie/es hat – he/she/it has
wir haben – we have
ihr habt – you all have (informal)
sie/Sie haben – they/you (formal) have

concepts.intro: sein links a subject to descriptions, identities, locations, and professions.
b: Identity: Ich bin Anna. – I am Anna.
Description: Er ist müde. – He is tired.
Location: Wir sind zu Hause. – We are at home.
Profession: Sie ist Lehrerin. – She is a teacher.
Age (important!): Ich bin 20 Jahre alt. – I am 20 years old (uses sein, not haben)

concepts.intro: haben expresses possession and appears in many fixed idiomatic expressions.
b: Possession: Ich habe ein Auto. – I have a car.
Hunger haben – to be hungry: Ich habe Hunger.
Durst haben – to be thirsty: Er hat Durst.
Angst haben – to be afraid: Sie hat Angst.
Zeit haben – to have time: Habt ihr Zeit?

concepts.intro: Both verbs are negated with nicht (or kein before a noun).
b: Ich bin nicht müde. – I am not tired.
Er hat keine Zeit. – He has no time.
Wir sind nicht zu Hause. – We are not at home.
Sie hat kein Auto. – She doesn't have a car.
nicht goes right after sein/haben when negating the whole idea

concepts.intro: sein and haben form the backbone of countless expressions and later grammar (like the perfect tense).
b: They cannot be conjugated with regular endings — they must be memorized as whole forms
Nearly every description of a person uses a form of sein
Nearly every possession or idiom uses a form of haben
Later, sein and haben are used as helping verbs for the past tense (Perfekt)
Mastering these two verbs early makes everything else easier

keyFacts: sein and haben are irregular and must be memorized form by form; they do not follow the regular -e/-st/-t pattern.
German expresses age with sein, not haben: Ich bin 20 Jahre alt (not 'Ich habe 20 Jahre').
Many physical/emotional states use haben + noun: Hunger haben, Durst haben, Angst haben.
sein and haben later double as helping verbs for the Perfekt (past) tense.
traps: Saying 'Ich habe 20 Jahre alt' instead of 'Ich bin 20 Jahre alt' — German uses sein for age, unlike Spanish/French.
Conjugating sein like a regular verb: 'er seint' or 'er ist' confusion — the correct form is simply er ist.
Mixing up du bist (sein) and du hast (haben) — they look similar but come from different verbs.
Saying 'Ich bin Hunger' instead of 'Ich habe Hunger' — hunger/thirst/fear use haben, not sein.

units.name: Word Order Basics

concepts.intro: In a German main-clause statement, the conjugated verb is always the second grammatical element, no matter what comes first.
b: Ich gehe heute ins Kino. – I go to the cinema today.
Heute gehe ich ins Kino. – Today I go to the cinema. (verb still 2nd)
The subject moves after the verb when something else is fronted
Only ONE element can come before the verb, even if it's a whole phrase
This is called 'inversion' and is required, not optional

concepts.intro: When a sentence has multiple adverbials, German orders them Time, then Manner, then Place.
b: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin. – I travel tomorrow by bus to Berlin.
morgen (time) → mit dem Bus (manner) → nach Berlin (place)
English often reverses this order, which trips up learners
TMP only applies when several adverbials appear together
Not every sentence needs all three

concepts.intro: Questions expecting yes or no are formed by putting the verb first.
b: Bist du müde? – Are you tired?
Spielst du Fußball? – Do you play soccer?
Haben Sie Zeit? – Do you have time?
No helper word like English 'do' is needed
The subject follows immediately after the verb

concepts.intro: Questions using a question word follow the pattern: W-word + verb + subject.
b: Wer bist du? – Who are you?
Was machst du? – What are you doing?
Wo wohnst du? – Where do you live?
Wann kommst du? – When are you coming?
Warum lernst du Deutsch? – Why are you learning German?

concepts.intro: Und, oder, aber, and denn connect two main clauses without changing word order in either clause.
b: Ich lerne Deutsch, und du lernst Englisch. – both clauses keep normal V2 order
aber (but): Ich bin müde, aber ich arbeite weiter.
oder (or): Kommst du, oder bleibst du hier?
denn (because/for): Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.
These are called 'coordinating' because they don't push the verb anywhere

concepts.intro: Weil, dass, and wenn introduce a subordinate clause and send the conjugated verb to the very end.
b: weil (because): Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
dass (that): Ich weiß, dass du müde bist.
wenn (if/when): Wenn du Zeit hast, ruf mich an.
The verb-last rule applies only inside the subordinate clause
This is one of the biggest word-order differences from English

keyFacts: The conjugated verb is always the second element in a German statement — this is the Verb-Second (V2) rule.
When time, manner, and place all appear, German orders them Time → Manner → Place.
Coordinating conjunctions (und, oder, aber, denn) do not change word order in the clauses they join.
Subordinating conjunctions (weil, dass, wenn) push the conjugated verb to the end of their clause.
traps: Saying 'Heute ich gehe' instead of 'Heute gehe ich' — fronting an element requires the verb to stay second, so the subject moves after it.
Keeping normal word order after weil: 'weil ich bin krank' is wrong — it must be 'weil ich krank bin' (verb last).
Forgetting verb-first order in yes/no questions: 'Du bist müde?' is casual/incorrect in writing — the standard question is 'Bist du müde?'.
Placing the place before the time: 'Ich fahre nach Berlin morgen' should follow TMP order as 'Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin'.

units.name: Family & Descriptions

concepts.intro: Core words for describing your family, each with its grammatical gender.
b: der Vater – father / die Mutter – mother
der Bruder – brother / die Schwester – sister
der Sohn – son / die Tochter – daughter
die Eltern – parents (always plural)
die Geschwister – siblings (always plural)

concepts.intro: Words for grandparents and other relatives.
b: der Großvater (Opa) – grandfather
die Großmutter (Oma) – grandmother
der Onkel – uncle / die Tante – aunt
der Cousin / die Cousine – male/female cousin
die Familie – family (die Familien in plural)

concepts.intro: Possessives like mein/dein/sein/ihr work like ein-words and agree with the noun that follows.
b: mein Vater (my father) / meine Mutter (my mother) / mein Kind (my child)
dein Bruder (your brother, informal)
sein Auto (his car) / ihr Auto (her car)
unser Haus (our house) / euer Hund (your-all dog)
The ending changes with gender/case, just like ein/eine/ein

concepts.intro: Adjectives placed after sein/werden describe the subject and never take an ending.
b: Er ist groß. – He is tall.
Sie ist freundlich. – She is friendly.
Das Kind ist klein. – The child is small.
Wir sind glücklich. – We are happy.
No agreement needed here — the adjective stays in its base form

concepts.intro: Adjectives placed directly before a noun DO take an ending that matches gender/case.
b: der große Vater – the tall father
die freundliche Mutter – the friendly mother
das kleine Kind – the small child
Compare: 'Er ist groß' (no ending) vs. 'der große Mann' (ending -e)
This ending system is learned gradually, but recognizing the pattern now helps later

concepts.intro: Combine sein + adjective, or use haben, to describe appearance and personality.
b: Er ist nett und freundlich. – He is nice and friendly.
Sie hat braune Augen. – She has brown eyes.
Mein Bruder ist jung. – My brother is young.
Meine Oma ist alt, aber aktiv. – My grandma is old but active.
Wie ist deine Familie? – What is your family like?

keyFacts: Possessive pronouns (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer) take the same endings as ein and must agree with the noun they modify.
Predicate adjectives (after sein) never take an ending: Er ist groß, not 'Er ist großer'.
Attributive adjectives (before a noun) do take an ending: der große Vater.
Eltern (parents) and Geschwister (siblings) are grammatically always plural in German.
traps: Writing 'meine Vater' instead of 'mein Vater' — der Vater is masculine, so the possessive stays mein, not meine.
Adding an ending to a predicate adjective, e.g. 'Er ist grosser' (which actually means 'taller') when you mean plain 'big/tall' — use 'Er ist groß'.
Confusing sein (the verb 'to be') with sein (the possessive 'his') — only context and capitalization patterns tell them apart.
Treating Eltern or Geschwister as singular — you cannot say 'ein Eltern'; these words have no singular counterpart with that meaning.

units.name: Food & Shopping

concepts.intro: Everyday food words, each with its article to memorize.
b: das Brot – bread / die Milch – milk
der Käse – cheese / das Wasser – water
der Apfel – apple / die Wurst – sausage
das Gemüse – vegetables (collective, singular in German)
der Zucker – sugar

concepts.intro: Polite, practical phrases used at a shop or market.
b: Ich möchte... – I would like... (polite)
Was kostet das? – How much does that cost? (singular item)
Was kosten die Äpfel? – How much do the apples cost? (plural)
Haben Sie...? – Do you have...? (formal)
Das ist alles, danke. – That's all, thank you.

concepts.intro: möchten is the polite way to say 'would like', more courteous than wollen (to want).
b: ich möchte – I would like
du möchtest – you would like (informal)
er/sie/es möchte – he/she/it would like
wir möchten – we would like
Ich möchte ein Brot, bitte. – I would like a loaf of bread, please.

concepts.intro: German plurals follow several patterns that must be learned with each noun.
b: Add -e: der Tisch → die Tische
Add -er (+ umlaut sometimes): das Buch → die Bücher
Add -n/-en: die Wurst → die Würste (umlaut), die Frau → die Frauen
Add -s (often loanwords): das Auto → die Autos
No change: der Apfel → die Äpfel (umlaut only)

concepts.intro: Expressions used to specify how much of something you want.
b: eine Flasche Wasser – a bottle of water
ein Kilo Äpfel – a kilo of apples
eine Tüte Milch – a carton/bag of milk
ein Stück Käse – a piece of cheese
German drops 'of': 'eine Flasche Wasser', not 'eine Flasche von Wasser'

concepts.intro: Vocabulary for talking about cost and paying.
b: das Geld – money / bezahlen – to pay
teuer – expensive / billig – cheap
die Kasse – checkout, cash register
der Supermarkt – supermarket
Das kostet drei Euro. – That costs three euros.

keyFacts: möchten (would like) is more polite than wollen (want) and is the standard verb for ordering or shopping.
German drops 'of' in quantity expressions: eine Flasche Wasser (a bottle of water), not 'eine Flasche von Wasser'.
Was kostet...? is used with singular items; Was kosten...? is used with plural items.
Plural formation has five main patterns (-e, -er, -n/-en, -s, or umlaut only) and must be memorized per noun.
traps: Saying 'Ich will ein Brot' in a shop — this sounds blunt/demanding; the polite form 'Ich möchte ein Brot, bitte' is preferred.
Inserting 'von' into quantities: 'eine Flasche von Wasser' is wrong — German simply says 'eine Flasche Wasser'.
Guessing the wrong plural ending, e.g. 'Autoen' instead of the correct 'Autos'.
Using 'kostet' with a plural subject: 'Was kostet die Äpfel?' should be 'Was kosten die Äpfel?'.

units.name: Daily Routine & Time

concepts.intro: Many daily-routine verbs have a prefix that detaches and moves to the end of the clause when conjugated.
b: aufstehen (to get up) → Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf.
anziehen (to put on/dress) → Sie zieht die Jacke an.
aufwachen (to wake up) → Er wacht früh auf.
fernsehen (to watch TV) → Wir sehen abends fern.
The prefix carries key meaning, so don't drop it — it just moves to the end

concepts.intro: The straightforward, digital way to tell time using 'Es ist... Uhr'.
b: Es ist ein Uhr. – It is one o'clock.
Es ist drei Uhr. – It is three o'clock.
Es ist neun Uhr fünfzehn. – It is 9:15.
Wie spät ist es? – What time is it?
Um wie viel Uhr...? – At what time...?

concepts.intro: Everyday spoken German uses halb, Viertel nach, and Viertel vor — these trip up English speakers.
b: Viertel nach zwei – quarter past two (2:15)
Viertel vor drei – quarter to three (2:45)
halb drei – half past two (2:30) — NOT half past three!
halb zwei – half past one (1:30)
German 'halb X' looks ahead to the NEXT hour, unlike English 'half past'

concepts.intro: Verbs and phrases for describing a typical day.
b: aufstehen – to get up / frühstücken – to eat breakfast
sich anziehen – to get dressed / duschen – to shower
zur Arbeit gehen – to go to work / arbeiten – to work
zu Abend essen – to eat dinner / schlafen gehen – to go to sleep
Ich stehe auf, dusche, und frühstücke. – I get up, shower, and eat breakfast.

concepts.intro: Different prepositions are used for clock times, days, and months.
b: um for clock time: um 8 Uhr (at 8 o'clock)
am for days: am Montag (on Monday)
im for months: im April (in April)
Days: Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag, Sonntag
am Wochenende – on the weekend

concepts.intro: Words that link the steps of a routine in order.
b: zuerst – first (of all)
dann – then
danach – after that
zum Schluss / zuletzt – finally / last
Zuerst stehe ich auf, dann dusche ich, danach frühstücke ich.

keyFacts: In a separable-prefix verb, the prefix detaches and moves to the very end of a main clause: Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf.
German 'halb zwei' means 1:30 (half BEFORE two), not 2:30 — it looks forward to the next hour.
Clock times use um (um 8 Uhr), days use am (am Montag), and months use im (im April).
Sequencing words like zuerst, dann, danach, and zuletzt organize a daily routine into a clear order.
traps: Saying 'Ich aufstehe um 7' — the prefix must split off: correct is 'Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf'.
Assuming 'halb zwei' means 2:30 — it actually means 1:30, since German counts toward the next hour.
Using 'in Montag' instead of 'am Montag' — days of the week take the preposition am, not in.
Forgetting the prefix entirely in a subordinate clause where it should stay attached: 'weil ich aufstehe früh' should be 'weil ich früh aufstehe' with 'aufstehe' as one word at the end.

quiz.q: What does 'Hallo' mean?
What does 'Guten Morgen' mean?
What does 'Guten Tag' mean?
What does 'Guten Abend' mean?
What does 'Gute Nacht' mean?
What does 'Auf Wiedersehen' mean?
What does 'Tschüss' mean?
What does 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' mean?
quiz.e: 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' means 'How are you? (formal)'.

quiz.q: What does 'Danke' mean?
What does 'Bitte' mean?
How do you say 'hello (informal)' in German?
How do you say 'good morning' in German?
How do you say 'good day / hello' in German?
quiz.e: 'good day / hello' is 'Guten Tag' in German.

quiz.q: How do you say 'good evening' in German?
How do you say 'good night' in German?
How do you say 'goodbye (formal)' in German?
How do you say 'bye (informal)' in German?
How do you say 'How are you? (formal)' in German?
quiz.e: 'How are you? (formal)' is 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' in German.

quiz.q: How do you say 'thank you' in German?
How do you say 'please / you're welcome' in German?
Which greeting is used only when saying goodbye at night, never to greet someone?
quiz.e: Gute Nacht (good night) is a farewell, not a greeting.

quiz.q: Which form of 'you' should you use with a stranger you just met?
quiz.e: Sie is the formal 'you', appropriate for strangers and formal situations.

quiz.q: What does 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' mean?
quiz.e: This is the formal way to ask how someone is doing.

quiz.q: Which word means both 'please' and 'you're welcome'?
quiz.e: Bitte serves double duty as 'please' and 'you're welcome'.

quiz.q: How is the German 'w' in 'Wasser' pronounced?
quiz.e: German w is pronounced like the English v sound.

quiz.q: How is the German 'z' in 'Zeit' pronounced?
quiz.e: German z is always pronounced as 'ts'.

quiz.q: What sound does 'ß' represent?
quiz.e: ß (Eszett) represents a sharp, unvoiced 's' sound.

quiz.q: Which vowel combination sounds like English 'eye', as in 'nein'?
Which vowel combination is a long 'ee' sound, as in 'wie'?
What must ALWAYS be capitalized in German, regardless of position in a sentence?
quiz.e: All German nouns are capitalized, unlike in English.

quiz.q: Which is the correct informal way to ask 'How are you?'
quiz.e: Wie geht's? is the informal, casual version.

quiz.q: What does 'Entschuldigung' mean?
quiz.e: Entschuldigung is used to apologize or get someone's attention.

quiz.q: Which pair are BOTH informal goodbyes?
quiz.e: Tschüss and Ciao are both casual, informal farewells.

quiz.q: Where does word stress usually fall in native German words?
quiz.e: Stress typically falls on the first syllable of native German words.

PART_A.q: Which word sends the verb to the end of its clause?
PART_A.e: Weil is a subordinating conjunction requiring verb-last order.

PART_A.q: Which is correct: 'Er ist ___' (he is friendly)?
PART_A.e: Predicate adjectives after sein take no ending.

PART_A.q: What is the correct possessive: '___ Mutter ist nett' (my mother)?
PART_A.e: Feminine noun takes -e: meine Mutter.

PART_A.q: Which is the polite way to order in a shop?
PART_A.e: Möchte is the polite form for ordering.

PART_A.q: Which question asks the price of a single item?
PART_A.e: Singular subject uses 'kostet'.

PART_A.q: What does 'halb drei' mean?
PART_A.e: Halb drei means 2:30 (half BEFORE three).

PART_A.q: Which sentence correctly places a separable verb?
PART_A.e: The prefix 'auf' moves to the end of the clause.

PART_A.q: What does 'Entschuldigung' mean?
PART_A.e: Entschuldigung means excuse me or sorry.

PART_A.q: What replaces 'die Katze' as a pronoun?
PART_A.e: Die Katze is feminine, replaced by 'sie'.

PART_A.q: What is the stem of 'kaufen'?
PART_A.e: Drop -en from the infinitive: kauf-.

PART_A.q: Which idiom uses haben to mean 'to be thirsty'?
PART_A.e: Durst haben is the correct idiom.

PART_A.q: What is the word order in a yes/no question?
PART_A.e: Yes/no questions begin with the conjugated verb, then the subject.

PART_A.q: What is the plural of 'der Bruder'?
PART_A.e: Der Bruder becomes die Brüder.

PART_A.q: What is the correct plural of 'das Auto'?
PART_A.e: Das Auto takes an -s plural.

PART_A.q: Which preposition is used with days of the week?
PART_A.e: Am is used with days: am Montag.

PART_A.q: Which is an appropriate greeting in the evening?
PART_A.e: Guten Abend is used in the evening.

PART_A.q: Which negation is correct for 'Ich habe ein Buch'?
PART_A.e: Kein negates nouns with an indefinite article.

PART_A.q: Which sentence is correctly negated: 'I don't learn German'?
PART_A.e: Nicht negates the verb/activity here.

PART_A.q: Which verb form is correct: 'sie ___ ein Auto' (haben)?
PART_A.e: Sie (she) hat is correct (singular er/sie/es form).

PART_A.q: Which order is correct for Time-Manner-Place?
o: Ich fahre mit dem Bus morgen nach Berlin.
Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin.
Ich fahre nach Berlin morgen mit dem Bus.
Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin mit dem Bus.
PART_A.e: Correct TMP order: morgen (time), mit dem Bus (manner), nach Berlin (place).

PART_A.q: What does 'die Eltern' mean?
PART_A.e: Die Eltern means parents (always plural).

PART_B1.q: Which response correctly uses 'Sie' with a stranger?
PART_B1.e: Formal address uses Sie with the -en verb ending.

PART_B1.q: Which is the correct accusative form of 'ein Tisch'?
PART_B1.e: Masculine ein becomes einen in the accusative.

PART_B1.q: What is the correct er-form of 'hören'?
PART_B1.e: Er/sie/es takes -t: er hört.

PART_B1.q: Which sentence uses sein correctly to describe location?
PART_B1.e: Sein expresses location: wir sind zu Hause.

PART_B1.q: Which sentence correctly uses a W-question?
PART_B1.e: W-question order: W-word + verb + subject.

PART_B1.q: Which possessive pronoun correctly matches 'sein Auto' (his car, neuter noun)?
PART_B1.e: Neuter nouns take no ending after sein: sein Auto.

PART_B1.q: What does 'eine Flasche Wasser' mean?
PART_B1.e: Eine Flasche Wasser means a bottle of water.

PART_B1.q: Which preposition goes with months?
PART_B1.e: Im is used with months: im April.

PART_B1.q: What sound does 'ü' make?
PART_B1.e: Ü has no English equivalent; say 'ee' with rounded lips.

PART_B1.q: Which article correctly completes 'die ___ ' as the plural of 'der Mann'?
PART_B1.e: Der Mann becomes die Männer in the plural.

PART_B1.q: Which is correct: 'ihr ___ Fußball' (spielen)?
PART_B1.e: Ihr takes -t: ihr spielt.

PART_B1.q: How do you say 'She has no time'?
PART_B1.e: Die Zeit is feminine, so keine Zeit is correct.

PART_B1.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'dass'?
o: Ich weiß, dass er müde ist.
Ich weiß, dass er ist müde.
Ich weiß, er dass müde ist.
Ich weiß, dass ist er müde.
PART_B1.e: Dass sends the conjugated verb to the end: dass er müde ist.

PART_B1.q: Which sentence correctly uses an attributive adjective?
PART_B1.e: Attributive adjective before neuter noun takes -e here: das kleine Kind.

PART_B1.q: What does 'billig' mean?
PART_B1.e: Billig means cheap.

PART_B1.q: What does 'zuerst... dann... danach' express?
PART_B1.e: These words sequence events in order: first, then, after that.

PART_B1.q: Which is a correct informal farewell?
PART_B1.e: Tschüss is an informal goodbye.

PART_B1.q: What gender is 'das Mädchen' and why?
PART_B1.e: Nouns ending in -chen are always neuter.

PART_B1.q: Which is correct: 'du ___' (arbeiten)?
PART_B1.e: Stems ending in -t insert -e-: du arbeitest.

PART_B1.q: What does 'aufstehen' mean?
PART_B1.e: Aufstehen means to get up.

PART_B2.e: Nicht negates the adjective after sein: er ist nicht müde.

PART_B2.q: Which conjunction is coordinating and does not affect word order?
PART_B2.e: Denn is coordinating, unlike weil/wenn/dass which are subordinating.

PART_B2.q: Which possessive is correct: 'unsere ___' (our children, plural)?
PART_B2.e: Plural nouns take -e after unser: unsere Kinder.

PART_B2.q: Which phrase correctly asks for the price of plural items?

PART_B2.e: Viertel vor drei means quarter to three, 2:45.

PART_B2.q: Which greeting fits the morning specifically?
PART_B2.e: Guten Morgen is used specifically in the morning.

PART_B2.q: Which article is used for all plural nouns?
PART_B2.e: Die is used for all plural nouns regardless of original gender.

PART_B2.q: What is the correct wir-form of 'machen'?

PART_B2.e: Ich habe Hunger is the correct idiom using haben.

PART_B2.q: Which sentence correctly places the verb after a fronted time expression?
PART_B2.e: Verb stays second: Heute lerne ich Deutsch.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

PART_C.q: Essay plan: identify the single most important takeaway of this course. Defend it using three units as evidence, then address one counterargument.
o: Clear thesis, three unit-specific pieces of evidence, genuine counterargument, resolution
PART_C.e: Full argumentative architecture earns top marks.
